stories.title: The Green Screen and the Hair Light
stories.description: The episode opens with technical banter about a natural green screen and a hair light placed 150 million kilometers away (a joke about the sun), showcasing how even basic production setup matters.
stories.insight: Details and preparation matter, even in casual conversations. Small things like proper lighting and green screens reflect care and professionalism.
stories.why_share_worthy: A light, human moment that humanizes the podcast hosts and shows the care that goes into production.

stories.title: The Privilege of Choice and the Responsibility to Think
stories.description: Amit reflects on how both he and Ajay grew up fortunate - with access to books, good lives, and the ability to travel. Yet they see poverty and problems in India, and this gap motivates their thinking about development.
stories.insight: Privilege comes with responsibility. If you've been fortunate, you have an obligation to think deeply about how to help others achieve the same.
stories.why_share_worthy: Connects personal privilege to intellectual purpose - why these conversations matter beyond abstract economics.

stories.title: Too Many People Get Stuck in a Groove
stories.description: Amit observes that many economics professionals adopt ideological packages and dogmas, following career paths without actually caring what's happening in the real world or whether their ideas work.
stories.insight: It's easy to become ideologically comfortable and stop questioning. Real development thinking requires continuous contact with reality and what actually works.
stories.why_matters: A critique of institutional economics and the ivory tower - where people defend positions for career reasons rather than truth-seeking.

recommendations.title: Understanding PPP (Purchasing Power Parity)
recommendations.author: Amit Varma (promised YouTube explanation)
recommendations.reason: PPP is essential for comparing standards of living between countries. This will be explained in both English and Bengali to make it accessible.
recommendations.notes: Foundational concept for understanding development measurement

recommendations.title: Development Economics Field
recommendations.author: Multiple scholars and practitioners
recommendations.reason: Understanding the landscape of development economics - what we know, what we don't, and what are the dead ends. This episode serves as an orientation to this field.
recommendations.notes: Not a single book but a field of inquiry worth exploring

core_ideas.explanation: Why is Indian per capita GDP one-tenth of the United States? (PPP-adjusted) This single question should guide all thinking about development policy and economics. It forces focus on what actually matters - living standards and human welfare.
core_ideas.why_matters: Gives purpose and direction to economic thinking. Every policy proposal should be evaluated against whether it helps reduce this gap.

core_ideas.idea: Development is About Real Lives, Not Just Numbers
core_ideas.explanation: Development economics isn't about fiscal deficits, inflation rates, or policy mechanisms. It's about real people, real poverty, real suffering. The numbers are just proxies for human welfare.
core_ideas.why_matters: Prevents becoming detached from the moral urgency of development work. You're not optimizing equations; you're trying to improve human lives.

core_ideas.explanation: It's dangerous to adopt an ideological package of beliefs that explains the world to you and makes you comfortable in your knowledge. This leads to defending ideas from dogma rather than from evidence.
core_ideas.why_matters: A warning against intellectual laziness. You must continually return to first principles and ask if your beliefs match reality.

core_ideas.idea: The Paragliding Metaphor - Understanding the Lay of the Land
core_ideas.explanation: Good development thinking requires both a sky-high view (understanding foundational frameworks and the big picture) and the ability to zoom in on specific problems. You need both.
core_ideas.why_matters: Orientation is as important as answers. Knowing where you are, what the terrain looks like, and what you're trying to achieve is more important than having ready-made solutions.

core_ideas.explanation: The fundamental question should animate all work in this field: How can we make India a better place for everyone? This should drive intellectual work, not career advancement or ideological commitment.
core_ideas.why_matters: Purpose clarifies thinking. When you remember why the work matters, you're less likely to get stuck defending bad ideas or ideologies.
